entries.clue: Appliances to cook with propane, possibly (4)

annotation.surface: Cookers in a farmhouse kitchen running off bottled gas.
annotation.walkthrough: An Aga is the heavy cast-iron range that sits permanently warm in a British kitchen, and the clue wants several of them. Propane supplies no letters of its own: it is there only to be called a gas.
annotation.definitionFit: Agas are cast-iron cooking ranges, a household name in Britain, so 'appliances to cook with' is the category they belong to.

entries.clue: Gold on the rise in fashionable club (4)

indicatorNotes.on the rise: Something on the rise is heading upwards, and in a down entry that means its letters are read from the bottom up.

OR is gold in heraldry, here climbing the grid

annotation.surface: The gold price climbing at a fashionable nightclub.
annotation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic name for gold and one of the first conventions worth learning. The club is not the nightspot of the surface but the one in a golf bag.
annotation.definitionFit: An iron is one of the metal-headed golf clubs used for the shorter approach shots, so 'club' is the group it sits in.

entries.clue: Issue in item after item (4)

indicatorNotes.in: What is found in something lies inside it, so the letters wanted are sitting within the words that follow.

blocks.note: ITEM set down after ITEM, and the four letters wanted run across the join between the two copies

annotation.surface: A complaint that keeps surfacing in one news item after another.
annotation.walkthrough: The hiding place is not on the page as printed: the instruction 'after' has to be carried out first and the word written twice, which shifts its first two letters round to the back. Issue and emit are both what a chimney does with smoke.
annotation.definitionFit: To emit is to send out — smoke, light, a sound — and 'issue' is the same verb, a thing flowing out from its source.

entries.clue: As discussed, hold what a setter needs to take the next steps? (4)

annotation.definition: what a setter needs to take the next steps

indicatorNotes.As discussed: Something taken as discussed is taken as it is said aloud, so the sound of the word matters and the spelling does not.

blocks.note: to hold something is to pause it, and that word spoken aloud gives these letters

annotation.surface: A crossword setter told to wait before working out the next stage.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter is the gun dog, not the person who wrote the puzzle, and the next steps are taken on four feet. A hold in a countdown is a pause.
annotation.definitionFit: A setter is a breed of dog, and a dog's feet are its paws, so the answer is what it walks on.

entries.clue: Naysayer checked up (6)

indicatorNotes.up: Up in a down entry means the letters are to be read from the foot of the grid upwards.

blocks.note: a horse that is reined is checked, and those six letters run upwards

annotation.surface: A background check being run on the man who keeps saying no.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Checked up' looks like one phrase and is two separate instructions: a word for checked, then the direction to read it in. Reining a horse is holding it back.
annotation.definitionFit: A denier is someone who denies a thing outright — a climate denier, a Holocaust denier — which is what a naysayer does.

entries.clue: Both hands cradling mellow brew (5)

indicatorNotes.cradling: To cradle something is to hold it in your arms, so the word that follows is held between the letters just named.

blocks.note: L and R are the abbreviations for left and right
to mellow is to age, which is what time does to wine and to temper

annotation.surface: Someone carrying a drink carefully in both hands.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mellow' is the verb here, not the adjective describing the drink. Left and right stay at opposite ends of the entry, which is what makes the container so easy to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: Lager is the pale, bottom-fermented beer that fills most British bars, and beer is brewed, so 'brew' is the drink it is one of.

entries.clue: Kept going wildly in love with diamonds (5,2)

indicatorNotes.wildly: Anything done wildly is done without order, so the letters beside it will not be found in the order printed.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
D is diamonds on a bridge scorecard, joined to the fodder

annotation.surface: A couple besotted with each other and with expensive jewellery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kept going' is the survival sense — carried on existing — rather than the sense of continuing to move. Diamonds is the card suit, which is where its single letter comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: To live on is to carry on existing after something that might have finished you, which is what keeping going means.

entries.clue: Great upset with a curtailed Mrs. Thatcher (8)

indicatorNotes.upset: Something upset has been knocked out of its arrangement, so the letters are to be rebuilt in another order.
indicatorNotes.curtailed: To curtail is to cut short at the end, so the last letter of the word comes off before anything else happens.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
the article taken as a single letter and added to the fodder
the title docked of its final letter

annotation.surface: A furious row with a Mrs Thatcher who has been cut off mid-sentence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mrs.' belongs to the wordplay, not to the name: the definition is the surname on its own, and the answer is the first name that goes with it. Margaret Thatcher was Britain's prime minister from 1979 to 1990.
annotation.definitionFit: Thatcher names the woman by her surname and the answer is her first name, the standard crossword way of asking for one half of a famous name.

entries.clue: Tried again before satisfactorily taking part (5)

indicatorNotes.taking part: Taking part of a thing is taking a piece of it and not the whole, so the letters wanted are a run inside the words given.

blocks.note: the five letters wanted run across the gap between the two words, picking up the end of the first and the start of the second

annotation.surface: Somebody having another go before they manage to join in properly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tried' is the examination sense of the verb — to sit a paper — which is why the past tense reads oddly on its own. In Britain a failed exam is resat the following year.
annotation.definitionFit: To resit an exam is to take it a second time after failing, so someone who resat it tried again.

entries.clue: Birds keep moving south to the other side (4)

indicatorNotes.to the other side: The other side of a word is its opposite end, so the letter named travels from the front of it round to the back.

blocks.note: to keep something is to save it
S is the compass abbreviation for south, and it is the letter that shifts

annotation.surface: Birds crossing over on their way south for the winter.
annotation.walkthrough: Aves is the Latin class name for birds, the heading on a zoologist's chart. South never leaves the word: it only changes ends, which is why the letters all survive.
annotation.definitionFit: Aves is the taxonomic class containing every bird there is, so the plural 'birds' is precisely what it names.

entries.clue: Vivaldi wrote a lot of these, anything but priestly at the core (5)

annotation.definition: Vivaldi wrote a lot of these
annotation.definitionNote: The setter defines by pointing rather than naming: 'these' is whatever the composer put on the page in quantity, so the phrase identifies the answer instead of standing in for it as a synonym would.

indicatorNotes.at the core: The core of a word is the middle of it, so only the letters at its very centre are taken.

blocks.note: anything but true means not true, so the phrase comes down to the one word
the two letters at the centre of the eight-letter word

annotation.surface: Vivaldi being described as anything but priestly.
annotation.walkthrough: Vivaldi was an ordained priest, known as the Red Priest for his hair, which is what gives the insult in the surface its sting. What a composer writes a lot of is notes.
annotation.definitionFit: Notes are the individual sounds a composer sets down on the stave, and a composer as prolific as Vivaldi produced them by the thousand.

entries.clue: Cut sunscreen after vacation? Irrational, looking back (4)

indicatorNotes.after vacation: A place that has been vacated has had everyone inside it leave, so only the letters at the two ends stay behind.
indicatorNotes.looking back: Looking back is looking the way you have come, so those letters are read in the opposite direction.

blocks.note: the word with everything between its first and last letters gone
pi is the irrational number every schoolchild meets, here turned round

annotation.surface: Giving up the sunscreen the moment the holiday ends, which looks daft in hindsight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vacation' is not the holiday the surface offers: it is the word for emptying a place out, and it empties the word before it. Pi runs to no end and repeats no pattern, which is what makes it irrational.
annotation.definitionFit: To snip is to cut with a short quick stroke of the scissors, the same action 'cut' names.

entries.clue: Case of doctor holding 50% of ribose for pharmacist? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: A doser is anyone who gives out doses rather than a qualified chemist, and the question mark is the setter admitting that the job named is only roughly what the word means.

indicatorNotes.Case of: The case of a thing is the shell round the outside of it, so only the first and last letters are kept.
indicatorNotes.holding: Whatever holds something keeps it inside, so the letters named next go within the letters before them.
indicatorNotes.50% of: Half a word is half its letters, and here it is the back half that is used.

blocks.note: the outside letters of the word, its case
the back three letters of the six-letter sugar

annotation.surface: A doctor's bag with half a sugar sample in it, meant for the chemist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case of' looks like the bag the doctor is carrying and is in fact the instruction to keep only the outside letters. Ribose is the sugar that gives RNA its R.
annotation.definitionFit: A doser is one who measures medicine out in doses, which is the pharmacist's job seen from the patient's side of the counter.

entries.clue: Solver occasionally recording loss of consciousness (5)

indicatorNotes.occasionally: Occasionally means every so often rather than throughout, so only every other letter of the word is taken.

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of the word
an EP is an extended-play record, longer than a single and shorter than an album

annotation.surface: A crossword solver noting down each time they nod off over the grid.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loss of consciousness' sounds like something a doctor would write down and means nothing more alarming than a night in bed. The EP turns up constantly in wordplay and is worth learning on sight.
annotation.definitionFit: Sleep is the ordinary nightly state in which awareness switches off, so the medical-sounding phrase describes it exactly.

entries.clue: Ran into road gripping hammer, naked (6)

indicatorNotes.gripping: Whatever grips a thing holds it inside, so the letters named next are enclosed by the ones before.
indicatorNotes.naked: A naked word has had its covering taken off, so the letters at either end of it go.

blocks.note: RD is the abbreviation on any British street sign
the word stripped of the letter at each end

annotation.surface: A naked man running out into the road clutching a hammer.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs on from 14 down into 19 down, so six letters are split across two short lights. 'Naked' does to the hammer exactly what the surface has already done to the man.
annotation.definitionFit: To ram something is to drive into it hard and deliberately, which is what a driver who ran into a wall has done.

entries.clue: Answer buried in rubbish, whichever way you look - every solution is something like this (7)

annotation.definition: every solution is something like this
annotation.definitionNote: The setter defines by pointing at the grid rather than by naming a thing: every answer in this puzzle reads as a word in both directions, as this one does, so the phrase identifies the answer instead of substituting for it.

indicatorNotes.buried in: What is buried in something lies inside it with letters on either side, so this piece goes in the middle.

blocks.note: rot is rubbish in the sense of nonsense, as in 'what utter rot'
the same three letters read the other way round, which is what the phrase instructs
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

annotation.surface: A written reply thrown out with the rubbish and still readable from any angle.
annotation.walkthrough: This is the clue that explains the puzzle: every entry in the grid turns into a word when read backwards, and the word for a thing that turns is itself the same both ways.
annotation.definitionFit: A rotator is something that turns, and each answer in this grid turns round into another word or, like this one, into itself.

entries.clue: Detector of speeding Lada cutting off learner in posh car (5)

indicatorNotes.cutting off: To cut something off is to lop it away, so the letter named goes from the word before it.

the cheap Soviet-built saloon that was a standing joke on British roads
L is the plate a British learner driver must display, and it is the letter cut away

annotation.surface: A Lada cutting up a learner driver who is out in something expensive.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is in the cars: the cheapest saloon on the road barging past the dearest. Radar is short for radio detection and ranging, and is itself the same word backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A radar gun is what the police point at passing traffic to measure its speed, so it is the detector of speeding.

entries.clue: Perhaps watch author entering exhausted after striking editor (5)

indicatorNotes.entering: Something entering a word goes inside it, so these letters are planted in the middle of what follows.

ED is the masthead abbreviation for editor, and it is the pair struck out
the person writing the clue is its author, so 'author' is ME

annotation.surface: An exhausted author walking into the office having just thumped the editor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Striking editor' reads as a journalist on the picket line and is an instruction to delete two letters. The author is the setter: ME is the crossword's oldest piece of self-reference.
annotation.definitionFit: A timer is any device that measures elapsed time, and a watch is one of them, which is what 'perhaps' is flagging.

entries.clue: Advance payment desired when banks withdraw (4)

indicatorNotes.withdraw: To withdraw is to take away and leave, so the letters named are removed from the word.

blocks.note: something desired is wanted
the banks of a word are its edges, and here they are W and D

annotation.walkthrough: 'Banks withdraw' is a financial headline in the surface and two separate instructions underneath it. The ante is the stake each poker player pays into the pot before a card is dealt.
annotation.definitionFit: The ante is the stake every poker player puts up before the hand begins, so it is money paid in advance of anything happening.

entries.clue: How a service professional might address crazy mother missing daughter (5)

annotation.definition: How a service professional might address
annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the word's use rather than standing in for it: madam is the form of address itself, and the woman being addressed is left unnamed.

indicatorNotes.missing: What is missing has gone from the word, so the letter named is not written down.

blocks.note: mad is crazy
a dam is an animal's mother, the word a breeder uses
D is the genealogist's abbreviation for daughter, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A shop assistant coping with a furious mother who has turned up without her daughter.
annotation.walkthrough: The mother is the animal one, a foal's dam as printed in any stud book, which is why the human family of the surface leads nowhere. A waiter using the word is being polite, not stuffy.
annotation.definitionFit: Madam is the polite form of address a waiter, receptionist or shop assistant uses to a woman customer.

entries.clue: See 14
Produced domestic broadcast (4)

annotation.walkthrough: 'Domestic' is the noun, not the adjective: the domestic was the servant who did the housework in a large British household. The two spellings are a standard homophone pair.
annotation.definitionFit: Something made has been produced — manufactured, put together, brought into being — so the two past tenses swap directly.

entries.clue: Give up on eating small pudding (7)

indicatorNotes.eating: Whatever is eating something has it inside, so the letter named goes within the word before it.

blocks.note: to desert somebody is to give up on them
S is the size on the label of a small shirt

annotation.surface: Deciding against even a small pudding.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain the pudding is the whole sweet course, whatever it turns out to be, not one particular dish. Desert and dessert are separated by the single letter the clue puts in.
annotation.definitionFit: In British usage 'pudding' names the sweet course at the end of a meal, which is what a dessert is.

entries.clue: Theatre agent returning after the opening of Amadeus to change the backdrop (7)

indicatorNotes.returning: Something returning comes back the way it went, so those letters are read from their far end.
indicatorNotes.after: What comes after a thing follows it, so this piece is written on the far side of the letter just taken.
indicatorNotes.the opening of: The opening of a word is where it starts, so only the letter at its front is used.

the first letter of the title
an agent is a rep, here turned round

annotation.surface: A theatrical agent slipping back in once Amadeus has opened.
annotation.walkthrough: Amadeus is Peter Shaffer's play about Mozart and Salieri, which is why the Independent sets it in italics. The same three letters do duty twice over, once each way round.
annotation.definitionFit: To repaper a room is to hang fresh wallpaper on it, and the wall behind you is the backdrop — a theatre word borrowed for a domestic job.

entries.clue: Let new enzyme at last inside cheese-maker's additive (6)

indicatorNotes.at last: At last means at the end, so only the final letter of the word before it is taken.

blocks.note: a flat that is let is rented
N is the standard abbreviation for new
the last letter of the word

annotation.surface: A new enzyme finally being allowed into the dairy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Let' is the landlord's verb and rent is what it comes to, which hides the four letters the rest of the clue opens up. Rennet really is an enzyme preparation, taken from a calf's stomach.
annotation.definitionFit: Rennet is the enzyme preparation a cheese-maker stirs into milk to curdle it, the first step in turning milk into cheese.

entries.clue: Offer to build, show and pay for house (3,2)

the spare-room sense, giving a guest a bed for the night

annotation.surface: A builder's tender covering the work, the display and the bill.
annotation.walkthrough: Five senses of the same two words in a row, with no wordplay at all underneath them: offer, build, show, pay for, house. The last is the spare-room sense, the one a friend needing a bed asks for.
annotation.definitionFit: Something offered at auction is put up for sale, and a guest given a bed for the night is put up too.

entries.clue: Competition in pub ending in bad language and drama? (5)

annotation.walkthrough: 'Bad language and drama' reads as one phrase about a row and splits neatly between the two halves of the wordplay. Darts is played on a board in the corner of most British pubs, in leagues that run all winter.

entries.clue: Discharge from nose not appropriate for anyone to see (4)

U is the British film certificate given to anything the whole family may watch, and it is the letter that goes

entries.clue: Repositories for rubbish clues (4)

blocks.note: the council dump on the edge of a British town, where household waste is taken by the carload
the hints and pointers that nudge somebody towards the thing they are after

annotation.surface: Bins for the crossword clues that did not work.
annotation.walkthrough: Read straight through, the clue offers somewhere to throw bad puzzles away and the join between its two halves is invisible. A tip is the British word for the council rubbish dump.
annotation.definitionFit: A tip is the dump where household rubbish is taken, and tips are also the hints that point a solver towards an answer.

entries.clue: Creed often ethical, but not entirely (5)

indicatorNotes.not entirely: Not entirely means the words give up only part of themselves, so the letters wanted are a run inside them.

blocks.note: the five letters wanted run across the join between the two words, starting three letters into the first

annotation.surface: A set of beliefs that is mostly, though not completely, moral.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' qualifies the ethics in the surface and marks the hiding place in the wordplay, doing both jobs in the same three syllables. The word is the same read backwards, which is why it is in this grid.
annotation.definitionFit: Both words name a belief held as true — a creed is the doctrine professed, a tenet a principle within it — and they stand in for each other freely.

entries.clue: Head over heels, finally passionate (4)

indicatorNotes.over: In a down entry what goes over a thing sits above it, so these letters come first.
indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points at the end of the word, so only its last letter is used.

the last letter of the word

annotation.surface: Somebody falling head over heels at long last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head over heels' is one idiom in the surface and three separate instructions underneath. Being nuts about somebody is the very infatuation that idiom describes, which is why the definition sits so quietly at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: To be nuts about something is to be wild about it, so 'passionate' is the same enthusiasm in politer words.

entries.clue: Bucket brigade called out (4)

indicatorNotes.called out: Something called out is said aloud, so it is the sound of the word that counts and not its spelling.

entries.clue: Lascivious stare led reader without fear inside (4)

indicatorNotes.without: Without a thing means it is not there, so the letters named are taken out.

annotation.definitionFit: A leer is a sidelong stare with unmistakable sexual intent, which is what 'lascivious stare' spells out.

entries.clue: Set one plus one between 50 and 500 (4)

annotation.definitionFit: To lay a thing down is to set it in place, and the past tenses match — a table that has been laid has been set.

entries.clue: Stepped another way around old pothole? (4,4)
